title: Google Business Profile Checklist for Med Spas: Categories, Services, Photos and Reviews
seoTitle: Google Business Profile Checklist for Med Spas
seoDescription: A practical Google Business Profile checklist for med spas: name, categories, services, photos, booking link, reviews and posts, plus how to keep treatment claims accurate.
excerpt: Your Google profile is often the first thing a client sees. Here is what a complete, accurate and compliant med spa profile looks like.
imageAlt: Clean, bright aesthetic treatment room with a teal treatment bed, a desk and two chairs
imageIdea: Real photo of an empty, well lit aesthetic treatment room, no clients, no procedure in progress and no brand logos.
author: The SocialDM Insights Team
bodyHtml:
A strong Google Business Profile for a med spa is complete, accurate and honest: the right categories, a services list that names every treatment you offer, real photos of your space and team, a working booking link, steady reviews with careful replies, and posts that never promise results. Get those right and Google has what it needs to show you for the treatments you want to grow, and clients have what they need to book.

This checklist covers each part of the profile, what good looks like, and where med spas tend to get into trouble with treatment claims, photos and reviews.

What should your business name and categories be?

Use your real business name exactly as it appears on your sign and website. Google's guidelines for representing your business say keywords and other unnecessary information are not allowed in the name and can lead to suspension. "Glow Aesthetics" is fine. "Glow Aesthetics Botox Fillers Laser Scottsdale" is not.

For categories, Google asks you to use as few as you need to describe your core business, to make the primary category as specific as possible, and not to use categories as keywords. Choose the primary category that matches what most clients come to you for, then add only the few that cover genuine core services. The treatments you want to grow belong in your services list and on your website.

How should a med spa list its services?

List every treatment you actually offer, by its plain name, with a short factual description. Google lets you add services from suggested options for your business type or create custom ones, and you can add descriptions and prices.

This is where treatment claims first creep in. Keep descriptions to what the treatment is, who performs it and what a consultation covers. Leave out words like "guaranteed," "permanent" or "painless," and do not promise outcomes. The FTC's Health Products Compliance Guidance says claims about the health benefits or safety of health related products need competent and reliable scientific evidence. Have your medical director approve every description before it goes live.

What photos should be on a med spa profile?

Real, recent photos of your exterior, entrance, reception, treatment rooms and team. Clients want to know what the place looks like before they walk in, and photos of the front door help first timers find you.

Google's photo guidelines say your business must be verified for photos to show, that photos should be JPG or PNG between 10 KB and 5 MB, and that they should look like the real place rather than being heavily altered, filtered or AI generated. Polished is fine. Misleading is not.

Before and after photos need extra care. Use them only with the client's written consent, keep them unretouched and representative, and never show a face without explicit permission for that specific use. If HIPAA applies to your practice, HHS says marketing uses of patient information generally require written authorization. HHS also settled with a physical therapy provider that posted testimonials with full names and full face photos without valid authorizations.

Should you add a booking link?

Yes, if you take online bookings. Google lets you add booking links to your profile, and some scheduling providers can connect bookings through Google directly. Test the link on a phone. It should land on a booking page for your location, not your home page, and it should still work after you change software.

How should a med spa handle reviews?

Ask every client the same way and reply in general terms. Google says more reviews and positive ratings can help local ranking, so a steady flow matters more than a burst.

The rules are clear. Google's Maps content policy says businesses may not offer incentives for reviews, discourage negative reviews or ask only happy clients. The FTC's rule on fake reviews and testimonials bans fake reviews and incentives tied to a particular sentiment. So no "$25 off for a five star review," and no review requests sent only after a client says they loved their results.

When you reply, never confirm that the reviewer is a client, name a treatment or discuss their results. A calm, general reply, with an invitation to call the practice directly, protects privacy and reassures the next person reading.

What should you post on Google?

Use posts for news, events and offers that are true and specific. Google's posts help page describes update, offer and event posts, and says posts older than six months are archived unless they have a date range. Its posts content policy says you are responsible for making sure your content complies with applicable laws.

For a med spa, that means an offer post should state the real terms, a new treatment post should describe what the treatment is rather than what it will do for someone, and photos should follow the same consent rules as everywhere else.

What about questions and AI answers in Maps?

Clients increasingly get answers from Google itself. Google says its Ask Maps feature works through reviews, photos, place details and the web to answer questions about places. How public questions appear on profiles has also been changing, so do not rely on one feature.

The safer approach is to make the answers easy to find everywhere: whether consultations are required, who performs injectables, how pricing works, parking and accessibility. Put them in your services, your website and, where your profile still shows questions, short factual answers.

What does a complete med spa profile look like?

Profile areaWhat good looks like
NameYour real business name, no keywords or city
CategoriesA specific primary category and only the few that describe core services
ServicesEvery treatment you offer, with plain, approved descriptions and no promised results
HoursRegular and holiday hours that match your website
PhotosReal, recent photos of the exterior, rooms and team; any client photos with written consent
BookingA link that opens a booking page for this location on a phone
ReviewsA steady flow from asking every client, with general, private replies
PostsCurrent, accurate news and offers with real terms

How do you keep the profile accurate and compliant?

Give one person ownership, and check the profile at least monthly and whenever something changes: a provider leaves, a treatment is added or retired, hours shift or you switch booking software.

Keep one approved source for treatment descriptions, and use it on your profile, website and social channels so every claim has been reviewed by your medical director. This is general guidance, not legal advice. For rules specific to your state and your treatments, talk to your own counsel.

Keeping profiles complete, accurate and consistent with your website is part of the work we do for aesthetic practices at The SocialDM. You can see how it fits together on our med spa marketing page.

Questions we hear

Can a med spa put treatment names in its Google business name?

No. Google's guidelines say your business name should match your real world name, and adding keywords or other unnecessary information is not permitted and can lead to suspension. Treatments belong in your services list and categories.

Can a med spa post before and after photos on its Google profile?

Only with the client's written consent and only photos that show realistic results. If HIPAA applies to your practice, HHS says marketing uses of patient information generally need written authorization.

Is it okay to offer a discount in exchange for a Google review?

No. Google's Maps content policy says businesses may not offer incentives such as payment or discounts for reviews, and the FTC's rule bans incentives tied to a particular sentiment.

Does adding a booking link to Google Business Profile help?

It makes booking one tap easier for a client who is ready. Google lets you add booking links to your profile, and some booking providers integrate with Google directly.

How often should a med spa update its Google Business Profile?

Check it at least monthly and any time something changes, such as hours, providers, treatments or your booking system. Small mismatches between your profile and website are the most common problem.

takeaways: Use your real business name with no keywords, a specific primary category and only the few categories that describe core services.
List every treatment in your services with plain, approved descriptions and no promised results.
Use real, recent photos, and post client photos only with written consent.
Google and the FTC both prohibit incentives tied to reviews; ask every client the same way and keep replies general.
Give one person ownership of the profile and check it monthly and whenever hours, providers, treatments or booking software change.
